$\hat{p}$ is read “p hat”: the hat indicates that it is an estimate drawn from the sample.

Read as: “p hat follows a normal with mean p and standard deviation the square root of p times one minus p over n”.

Where it comes from: the number of successes $X$ is a [[pe-binomial|binomial]] $B(n, p)$, with mean $np$ and deviation $\sqrt{np(1-p)}$. Dividing by $n$ divides both, and for large $n$ the binomial is [[pe-normal|approximated by a normal]].

Pierre-Simon Laplace hizo en 1786 lo que: In 1786 Pierre-Simon Laplace did what would today be called a sample survey, without surveying anybody. They wanted to know how many inhabitants France had without running a census, which cost a fortune. They counted the inhabitants of a few parishes spread across the country and the births those parishes recorded, computed the proportion, and applied it to the births of the whole kingdom, which were written down. They estimated some 28 million and, more remarkably, also computed the probability of being wrong by more than half a million: it was the first time anyone accompanied an estimate with its margin of error.
